newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Prodi urges "quick, transparent" Albania elections.
newsitem.headline: Prodi urges "quick, transparent" Albania elections.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi, fresh from a rapturous welcome in the rebel-held port of Vlore, said Sunday that an Italian-led security force would help pave the way for fair elections in Albania.
"Italy wants to help Albania to reconstruct the state and to have quick democratic, transparent elections," he told a joint news conference with Prime Minister Bashkim Fino.
"I don't want to interfere in internal Albanian policy. We are not here to ... make the situation worse."
Italy has been at pains to stress it has no political motives since a junior foreign minister caused a storm last week by suggesting President Sali Berisha should leave office.

Prodi's flying visit came as an Italian-led security force was due to start arriving en masse in the port of Durres Tuesday to protect shipments of aid after weeks of violent unrest sparked by the collapse of popular savings schemes.
Prodi, escorted by heavily-armed Italian marines, arrived in Vlore to express his condolences after a boat disaster last month in which more than 80 Albanian refugees were feared dead.
Thousands of cheering Albanians lined the road as Prodi's motorcade swept past and some 10,000 packed a square outside a university building where he and Fino met local leaders.
"The mission is called 'Alba' (dawn)," Prodi told a news conference in Vlore. "And this could be the dawn in the history of Albania, the rebirth of Albania."

The 6,000-strong U.N.-backed force, the first of its kind to be led by Italy, has no mandate to disarm rebels who seized control of many southern towns in an outpouring of rage last month following the collapse of popular savings schemes.
Advance troops from the multinational mission began arriving in Albania last week.
"We have to be very clear that our mission is a mission for helping the civil Albanian society to reconstruct itself," Prodi said in Tirana.
"Our objective is to go home as soon as we have helped the reconstruction of the Albanian state and one month after the holding of democratic elections," he said.
Berisha, blamed by many Albanians for sparking the crisis by allowing the dubious savings schemes to flourish unchecked, has agreed to early elections due by the end of June.

Crowds in Vlore, home of many of the schemes, chanted insults against Berisha, a northerner. Fino said he was proud of the welcome given to Prodi, where there had been fears of an anti-Italian backlash after the boat disaster.

Tirana said that more than 80 people were killed when the boat, which had left Vlore packed with refugees fleeing violence, was rammed by the Italian ship, charges Italy denies. It was the worst maritime disaster in modern Albania's history.

Prodi planned to visit Vlore last week, but that was postponed because of a new outbreak of violence. The southern town has been under rebel control since the start of the armed uprising in which nearly 300 people have been killed.
Prodi said Italy planned to open a consulate in Vlore and that the two countries would work together to encourage foreign investment in Albania.

"This is a country of immense potential," Prodi said. "It has had a crisis. I hoped for a while that it could get over it alone. It has asked for our help. We'll give it, but I believe this country is capable of making great strides forward. It just needs a rebuilt state, through democratic elections."
